gaps.fact: Ale yeast is Saccharomyces cerevisiae, warm and fast at 68 to 72°F (20 to 22°C); lager yeast is Saccharomyces pastorianus, cool and slow at 48 to 55°F (9 to 13°C). The Village Beer & Cider chapter names both species, but no stem in either bank asks them for beer (the one stem keyed S. cerevisiae, r-el5pbcck, is about wine), and the Court's two temperature bands appear nowhere (i-h0tt4xg5 puts twenty and ten degrees in its stem).

The Court's American hops are Cascade, Centennial and Citra. Cascade is keyed once (i-cm885u58) and the European trio of Hallertau, Saaz and Tettnang once (c-dmz3kpg5); Centennial and Citra are never named anywhere in the Codex.
Water is over 90 per cent of beer. No chapter or stem gives the figure (the sake chapter's four fifths is the only such line in the Codex).

At least two producers for each of the Court's ten styles: European Pale Lager, American Pale Lager, Pilsner, American IPA, American Pale Ale, American or British Porter, Irish Dry Stout, Hefeweizen, Witbier, Sour Beer. The Village chapter names Pilsner Urquell, Guinness and five Belgian Trappist breweries; no stem keys a producer to a style, and nothing names a producer of American IPA, American Pale Ale, porter, Hefeweizen, Witbier, sour beer or an American or European pale lager.
Beer is one of the oldest alcoholic beverages. Never said in either chapter or any stem.
Mesopotamia: hunter gatherers settled to farm and grew grain for bread and beer. The Codex's beer history starts at the 1516 purity law; Mesopotamia is never named.

Name and shape of the pint, mug, tulip, pilsner and weizen glass. Only the goblet is keyed (c-7rxt7gzu); i-83m5hvrr names a tulip and a weizen glass in its stem but asks what a glass does, and the serviceRef glassware row lists pilsner, tulip or goblet and nonic pint; the mug is never taught and no stem matches a glass to a style.

The Court's four pairing principles: sweetness from malt, bitterness from hops, generally low alcohol, carbonation. The Codex teaches roast with char and bitterness against sugar; carbonation and modest alcohol as beer's strengths at the table are never taught or asked.

Beer containers (bottle, can, keg in many sizes) and keg costing: a Quarter Barrel keg holds 29.3 litres or 992 ounces, and the Court's worked example (200 guests, 40 per cent take one 16 ounce pint: 80 pints, 1,280 ounces, so two quarter barrels) has no counterpart. No stem names a keg size or costs beer.

notes: Mapped questions: Régionale 56 (Beer), Village 20 (Beer & Cider, of which 14 are on beer and 6 on cider and perry), 76 in all and 70 on beer. Two further beer stems sit in Service & Hospitality (c-m36084ry, the beer clean glass; c-bj2f7v48, FIFO). The Régionale bank carries most of the Court's Certified beer column (malting, kilning, mashing, the boil, lagering, ABV, IBU), while the Village Beer & Cider cat is pitched above the Court (decoction, hop creep, krausening, soft spiles, keeving) and asks none of the Court's Certified lines on yeast species, producers, glass names, pairing principles or keg costing. Every one of the Court's 10 rows has a chapter fact or a stem, but the Producer row rests on one chapter line and the Business row on FIFO alone. Read with care in our own copy: the serviceRef glassware row gives a nonic pint of 568 ml, the imperial pint, while the Court's costing uses a 16 ounce US pint (473 ml); an e- costing question should state its pint. The Court's 'Ingredients' cell lists oats among the grains and the Codex never mentions oats outside a distractor (oatmeal stout, i-rahubs3x), a small omission not logged as a gap. No law or classification change since 8.2023 touches these rows; no search was spent.
